mission: Search for source-bound physical correlates of Osirian body-part traditions using the chain BODY_PART_TEXT -> CONTAINER -> EXCAVATED_OBJECT -> MUSEUM_PASSPORT -> IMAGING_CONTENT, without promoting ritual proxies into literal biological relics.

qh207.site: Qubbet el-Hawa, tomb QH 207, opposite Aswan
qh207.interpretive_context: Casting-workshop/depot assemblage associated with Late Period reuse of QH207; exact micro-context of individual pieces was not recorded in sufficient detail.

production_B1.finding: Moulds consistently preserve already-cast and broken bronze feet/tenons of Osiris statuettes topped with new wax bodies before remoulding.
production_B1.importance: Direct material evidence for ancient handling/re-use/reconstruction of broken Osiris-image body parts, independent of any literal divine-body claim.

QH207_32.description: Osiris statuette, wax body plus bronze/copper foot segment; height about 13.2 cm.
QH207_32.archive_note: Fundbuch says: Osiris statuette from a mould, modelling material with copper foot; 'foot glued on by A.E.'
QH207_32.A_E_candidate: Angelika Edel is documented as a member of the Bonn 1969 excavation team; therefore the glue notation raises a modern-reassembly control that must be resolved from the archive before using the physical interface itself as ancient evidence.
QH207_32.firewall: QH207/32 is not required to establish the broader ancient broken-foot phenomenon because QH207/38-40 and /55 independently preserve bronze feet inside ancient moulds.

QH207_38.description: Casting mould for four Osiris figures; X-ray showed bronze concentrated in foot regions.
QH207_38.current_location: not findable in later Bonn inventory

QH207_51.description: Casting mould for two Osiris statuettes containing differently complete bronze foot fragments with damaged tenons plus upper-body/head fragments; probable wax reconstruction between pieces.
QH207_51.importance: This is now a stable museum-passport target for direct conservation/imaging follow-up rather than a lost generic QH number.

heracleopolis.textual_target: Papyrus Chester Beatty VIII describes buttocks, penis, legs and posterior/vital parts of Osiris in a great acacia-wood chest/reliquary at Heracleopolis.
heracleopolis.archaeological_target: Recover any actual box/casket/shrine/reliquary, closed deposit, wrapped organic package, grouped broken Osiris figures, djed deposit or object with cavity/content from Ehnasya/Ihnasya contexts that can be joined to a secure excavation record.

2026_sca.finding: Reused stone block with royal names of Senusret III and a cartouche naming Osiris-Naref recovered by the SCA mission at Ihnasya El-Madina.
2026_sca.effect: Confirms physical inscriptional presence of the Osiris-Naref cult at Ihnasya, but reuse prevents treating the block itself as a fixed sanctuary locator.

petrie_1904_side_target.published_object: Roman Ehnasya, plate XLVIII no. 65, labelled 'Osiris vase'
petrie_1904_side_target.interpretive_ceiling: The label may denote an Osiris-Canopus cult image; vessel form does not establish relic contents.

heracleopolis.spanish_mission_control: Heracleopolis excavations have yielded ordinary funerary containers such as canopic jars; reported examples from circa 800-700 BCE can be empty, illustrating that ritual container presence does not imply preserved organ contents.
